Below is a synthesis of when BYOD implementations tend to fail in large, high‑stakes university exams (500+ students), and how institutional factors produce conflicting recommendations in the literature.

Summary of the problem and why it matters
- BYOD for exams promises cost savings and scalability but hinges on stable infrastructure, robust supervision, careful exam design, and clear policies. In practice, success or failure often pivots on whether institutions can guarantee device neutrality, reliable connectivity and power, prompt technical support, and equitable accommodations at scale. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Institutions should pilot the format, train users, invest in reliable wireless and power, implement rigorous supervision/monitoring, and revise policies with explicit contingencies</cite>.

When BYOD implementation fails in large, high‑stakes exams
1) Scalability limits of proctoring and technical fragility
- Human and algorithmic proctoring degrade when candidate counts, device heterogeneity, and network strain are high; even “low” incident rates can paralyze operations if each incident costs substantial staff time. <cite id="330c8581-3">The major weakness of proctored systems lies in technical failures and lack of user experience; complex apps and multicomponent exams require very performant gear; one technical issue interrupted a candidate’s exam, revealing vulnerability to the low quality of personal gear</cite>. <cite id="330c8581-3">A 12‑person proctoring team detected all suspicious events but solved relatively few technical issues, revealing low system efficiency</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Proctoring at scale demands explicit accessibility‑centered workflows; the field shifted rapidly from in‑person to online proctoring with little guidance on choosing proctoring types for diverse learners</cite>.
- BYOD success depends on supervision capacity and venue availability, not just software. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Feasibility was limited mainly by venue capacity and supervision resources, without increasing grading workload</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Lockdown browsers and automated video proctoring are common controls, but they increase client device demands and introduce new failure surfaces</cite>.

2) Device heterogeneity and connectivity/power constraints
- BYOD exams can be “secure” only if institutions standardize the environment; otherwise, uneven OS/browser versions, local network bandwidth, battery life, and hardware capability drive uneven performance and reliability. <cite id="330c8581-3">Technical issues were mainly software‑related and the system was vulnerable to the low quality of personal gear</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Safe Exam Browser and related lockdown approaches restrict unauthorized software and internet access, but require disciplined client configuration and monitoring</cite>.
- Network and power are not optional for hundreds to thousands of devices. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Institutions should invest in secure and robust infrastructure, including reliable wireless connectivity and power solutions</cite>. Absent such controls, BYOD exams suffer from dropped sessions, slow load times, and abrupt shutdowns during invigilation.

3) Accessibility, accommodations, and integrity trade‑offs
- BYOD and remote proctoring can conflict with disability‑related accommodations and principles of equitable design; institutions without mature accessibility processes risk legal and pedagogical harm even as they deploy integrity tools. <cite id="c05e43de-0">A decade of experience in disability‑related testing accommodations led to a framework for equitable online proctoring and negotiated vendor practices</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-1">BYOD success requires meticulous setup: tailored exercise variants, anomaly detection, and accommodations (time extensions, special seating) via examination boards to ensure fairness</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-2">Faculty worry about “unfair advantages” when remote arrangements alter timing, while eye control by proctors can be circumvented by concealed smartphones; online campus invigilation raises new self‑assistance risks</cite>.
- Lockdown and video proctoring can impede accessibility or create undue stress; without parallel in‑person or alternative modality accommodations, BYOD risks violating UDL and anti‑discrimination obligations. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Automated video proctoring detects screen changes to infer movement outside the window, adding usability burdens and potential misclassification risks for disabled students</cite>.

4) Integrity vs. learning outcomes and fairness trade‑offs
- Aggressive proctoring and monitoring can lower performance or inflate anxiety, undermining validity and equity. <cite id="c0a3d29a-4">Students performed 10–20% better but took roughly twice as long on non‑proctored vs. proctored exams; the effect persisted when comparing the same exam proctored vs. non‑proctored</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-3">Supervisor apps accurately detected suspicious events without affecting exam performance, but the system’s efficiency was low and technical issues could interrupt exams</cite>. Institutions that push continuous, intrusive monitoring without compensating for usability and time burdens risk depressing scores and alienating students.

5) Policy gaps, contingency planning, and vendor dependence
- BYOD policies that ignore device diversity, acceptable browsers/OS updates, emergency rollback, and student support lead to crisis management during invigilation. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Revising exam policies to include provisions and contingency plans for BYOD is crucial; supervisors should assist with technical issues and re‑routine students to labs if problems persist</cite>.
- Overreliance on proprietary proctoring suites can create lock‑in on privacy, auditability, and accommodations. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Institutions negotiated with vendors and led transitions to new practices while prioritizing accessibility, reflecting the need to align policy and vendor contracts with student needs</cite>.

What explains conflicting recommendations in the literature?
- Context and capacity shape guidance: “Pilot and iterate” vs. “deploy immediately with heavy monitoring”
  - Evidence from large cohorts shows that BYOD is feasible and can reduce dishonesty compared to fully remote proctored settings, but only with careful planning, supervision, and infrastructure—leading to a conservative, pilot‑first recommendation. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">BYOD showed reduced dishonesty compared to remote exams and is feasible at scale when venue capacity and supervision are adequate</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Pilots, training, robust infrastructure, supervision, and revised policies are recommended</cite>.
  - Conversely, studies documenting integrity breaches in BYOD and strong advisories to lock down devices and monitor students push toward proactive, technically and organizationally intensive controls—creating tension with accessibility and usability. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Allowing BYOD raises cheating concerns; recommended safeguards include lockdown browsers and automated video proctoring</cite>.
- Pedagogy and assessment design mediate technology choice
  - If exams are ill‑designed for device‑based work (e.g., copy‑pasteable resources), BYOD can increase invalid advantage; if well‑designed for higher‑order skills, BYOD can preserve validity. Institutions that rush to BYOD for “secure” invigilation without redesigning assessments invite failure. <cite id="c0a3d29a-1">Lockdown browsers restrict programs and internet; automated video proctoring detects screen changes</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">BYOD exams can emphasize higher cognitive levels, but instructors must balance difficulty and avoid over‑reliance on accessible tools; test runs with students are recommended</cite>.
- Legal/ethical obligations and diversity of learners
  - Accessibility frameworks urge accommodation‑first design and flexible modalities; integrity frameworks urge uniform monitoring; reconciling them requires nuanced policy and staffing. <cite id="c05e43de-0">A framework for equitable online proctoring prioritized accessibility and guided selection of proctoring types to fit student needs</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-2">Faculty perceive fairness risks when timing is graded; unchecked devices enable web self‑assistance and photo dissemination, complicating integrity in online settings</cite>.
- Infrastructure and cost realities
  - Well‑resourced institutions can invest in secure labs, stable Wi‑Fi, power backup, and trained proctoring teams and report scalable success; under‑resourced institutions may be advised to “use BYOD to save costs,” yet lack the infrastructure and supervision needed, which leads to failure. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Feasibility is limited by venue capacity and supervision resources; investing in robust infrastructure, training, and supervision is recommended</cite>. <cite id="330c8581-3">Education institutes should guarantee a fair and safe exam environment by offering high‑quality infrastructure and logistics, as low device quality can crash exams</cite>.
- Vendor ecosystems and measurement differences
  - Different proctoring vendors and platforms yield different failure modes and user burdens; literature often reports “success” under controlled vendor deployments while independent audits reveal usability and privacy risks. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Proctoring managers negotiated vendor contracts and transitioned practices to prioritize accessibility</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-1">Proctoring vendors provide live or AI‑driven review; process planning and data security are emphasized</cite>.
- Outcome orientation
  - Integrity-only studies recommend heavy monitoring to deter dishonesty; educational outcome studies find penalties to performance and time, producing conflicting guidance that depends on whether an institution prioritizes detection of misconduct or preservation of construct validity. <cite id="c0a3d29a-4">Non‑proctored exams yielded 10–20% higher scores but took twice as long; proctored vs. non‑proctored comparisons showed consistent performance penalties</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Various cheating‑prevention techniques exist, but they impose usability and fairness trade‑offs</cite>.

Practical institutional determinants to manage risk (decision checklist)
- Readiness and governance
  - Pilot in a representative cohort; freeze logistics (rooms, Wi‑Fi SSIDs, power) early; require dry‑runs with proctoring and monitoring; define escalation paths. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Start with a pilot; train faculty and students; revise exam policies with contingencies</cite>.
- Infrastructure and operations
  - Provide backup Wi‑Fi channels, bandwidth reservations, and power redundancy; stock exam rooms with chargers/USB, surge protectors, and quick‑swap devices; maintain a staffed help desk during exams. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Invest in reliable wireless connectivity and power solutions</cite>. <cite id="330c8581-3">Guarantee high‑quality infrastructure and logistics to avoid candidate gear‑quality failures</cite>.
- Security and integrity
  - Use client‑side lockdown browsers with strict plugin/USB/device policies; prefer local human proctoring for large cohorts with video streaming; document opt‑out accommodations and their monitoring constraints. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Safe Exam Browser turns student devices into secure workstations; automated video proctoring compares screen frames to detect movement</cite>.
- Accessibility and accommodations
  - Adopt a UDL/accommodation policy: allow approved assistive software/hardware; permit invigilated on‑site BYOD with extended time or separate room as alternatives; coordinate with disability services to pre‑approve plans. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Equitable online proctoring prioritized accessibility across diverse learners</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-1">Special seating, time extensions, and individual accommodations can be arranged within BYOD processes</cite>.
- Assessment design and validity
  - De‑emphasize copy‑paste tasks; require local reasoning traces; randomize items or variants; include anti‑collusion items; run test‑runs with students to calibrate time and tooling. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">BYOD exams should target higher cognitive levels; test runs with students help refine design and prevent over‑length/over‑difficult tasks</cite>.
- Vendor and policy alignment
  - Define audit rights and obligations: student consent for video, data retention, cross‑border transfers; specify recourse for false positives; reserve right to in‑person proctoring; mandate privacy impact assessments. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Institutions negotiated vendor practices to align with accessibility and proctoring goals</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-1">Security and protection of exam content and student data are essential in online exams</cite>.

Resolving the tension between success stories and pitfalls
- Success stories typically come from institutions that made compensating investments: secure rooms, dedicated IT support, trained proctoring staff, accessible workflows, and careful exam redesign. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">BYOD exams at scale are feasible if venue and supervision capacity are adequate; infrastructure and supervision are key</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-1">Proctoring software supports review by faculty/TAs or vendors, with processes for scheduling, monitoring, and scoring</cite>. <cite id="330c8581-3">BYOD systems can accurately detect suspicious behavior but are vulnerable to candidate device quality, revealing low system efficiency relative to demand</cite>.
- Pitfalls arise when institutions adopt BYOD primarily to cut costs or restore perceived “control,” without addressing device heterogeneity, accessibility obligations, and staffing/contingency capacity; this yields usability failures, integrity gaps, and fairness harms. <cite id="330c8581-3">Technical failures and user experience issues dominate weaknesses in proctoring systems; low gear quality can interrupt exams</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-4">Proctoring can depress performance by 10–20% and double exam time, indicating unintended construct‑validity damage</cite>.

Actionable takeaways for 500+‑student exams
- Do not default to BYOD without a parallel plan for supervised, wired exam rooms and a trained help desk; reserve BYOD for contexts where on‑site lab capacity is insufficient, and keep cohorts small enough for human proctoring. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Venue capacity and supervision resources are the binding constraints</cite>. <cite id="330c8581-3">Guarantee high‑quality infrastructure and logistics to prevent candidate gear failures</cite>.
- If using BYOD, standardize the client environment via lockdown browsers and pre‑install vetted IDEs/libraries; require device health checks (OS updates, camera/microphone permissions, battery level) and provide on‑site loaner devices and charging. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Lockdown browsers limit unauthorized apps/system functions/internet; BYOD with such controls plus web IDEs has been implemented for ~500 students</cite>.
- Build a risk‑based accommodation pathway: pre‑approve assistive technologies; allow supervised device swaps; offer adjacent‑room invigilation for disabilities or connectivity aversion; document alternatives to video proctoring. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Accessibility‑centered proctoring workflows support diverse learners</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-1">Special seating and time extensions can be arranged within BYOD processes</cite>.
- Calibrate monitoring intensity and time budgets; pair AI proctoring with human oversight, and sunset continuous, intrusive monitoring for low‑risk courses; monitor exam performance deltas and iterate on design. <cite id="c0a3d29a-4">Proctoring increased scores by 10–20% but doubled time; this suggests monitoring can change the construct being measured</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-3">Supervisor apps accurately detected suspicious events without harming performance, but the system’s efficiency was low</cite>.
- Publish a transparent BYOD policy: consent, privacy, failure modes, appeal process for false positives, and contingency “Plan B” (reserved lab seats, supervised device fallback). <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Revising exam policies to include provisions and contingency plans is crucial</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-1">Proctoring processes should include scheduling, monitoring, and scoring safeguards to maintain integrity and data security</cite>.

Remaining gaps and how to close them
- Institutions often lack post‑hoc audits tying BYOD to learning outcomes and fairness across demographics; establish blinded comparisons between proctored and non‑proctored versions of the same exam and analyze subgroup effects. <cite id="c0a3d29a-4">Empirical comparisons show 10–20% higher performance under non‑proctored conditions, suggesting potential validity trade‑offs</cite>.
- BYOD failure modes evolve with device ecosystems and vendor updates; maintain a continuous improvement loop with student advisory councils and disability services to surface accessibility regressions. <cite id="c05e43de-0">A framework for technology‑as‑a‑proctoring‑solution evolved from years of practice prioritizing accessibility and vendor negotiation</cite>. <cite id="330c8581-3">Technical issues were software‑driven and impacted candidate gear; institutions should guarantee infrastructure and logistics</cite>.

Bottom line
- BYOD implementation fails in large, high‑stakes exams when institutions skip infrastructure readiness, under‑staff supervision, ignore device heterogeneity and accessibility, and over‑monitor assessments without redesigning for validity. <cite id="330c8581-3">Proctoring weaknesses are dominated by technical failures and UX issues, revealing vulnerability to candidate gear quality</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Feasibility is ultimately bounded by venue capacity and supervision resources</cite>. 
- Conflicting recommendations stem from different institutional realities and objectives: accessibility and pedagogy demand accommodation‑first, usability‑aware designs; integrity regimes push for strict monitoring; reconciling them requires governance, infrastructure, and training investments, plus careful assessment redesign and transparent policies. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">BYOD reduced dishonesty relative to remote exams and is feasible at scale with robust infrastructure and supervision</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-4">Yet proctoring can depress performance and inflate time, indicating trade‑offs</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Accessibility‑centered frameworks show how to align proctoring choices with diverse learner needs</cite>. Institutions that treat BYOD as purely a technology deployment rather than a system change are most likely to see failures despite positive case studies. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Success depends on technology and policies and support mechanisms; lockdown browsers and automated video proctoring must be complemented by training and supervision</cite>.

With appropriate examination room infrastructure and availability, combined with an effective exam system, BYOD exams can be seamlessly scaled to accommodate over 1500 students simultaneously. Artemis enhances the examination process for both students and instructors, offering familiar usability for students, while providing instructors with helpful features such as (semi-) automatic assessment, plagiarism detection, exercise variants, session anomaly detection, and more. 

Computer-based exams with BYOD emphasize applying knowledge at higher cognitive levels, moving beyond rote memorization or basic comprehension of course content. In this article, we describe a BYOD exam solution based on lockdown browsers, software which temporarily turns students' laptops into secure workstations with limited access to applications, system functions, or the internet. Below is a synthesis of when BYOD implementations tend to fail in large, high‑stakes university exams (500+ students), and how institutional factors produce conflicting recommendations in the literature.

Summary of the problem and why it matters
- BYOD for exams promises cost savings and scalability but hinges on stable infrastructure, robust supervision, careful exam design, and clear policies. In practice, success or failure often pivots on whether institutions can guarantee device neutrality, reliable connectivity and power, prompt technical support, and equitable accommodations at scale. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Institutions should pilot the format, train users, invest in reliable wireless and power, implement rigorous supervision/monitoring, and revise policies with explicit contingencies</cite>.

When BYOD implementation fails in large, high‑stakes exams
1) Scalability limits of proctoring and technical fragility
- Human and algorithmic proctoring degrade when candidate counts, device heterogeneity, and network strain are high; even “low” incident rates can paralyze operations if each incident costs substantial staff time. <cite id="330c8581-3">The major weakness of proctored systems lies in technical failures and lack of user experience; complex apps and multicomponent exams require very performant gear; one technical issue interrupted a candidate’s exam, revealing vulnerability to the low quality of personal gear</cite>. <cite id="330c8581-3">A 12‑person proctoring team detected all suspicious events but solved relatively few technical issues, revealing low system efficiency</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-0">Proctoring at scale demands explicit accessibility‑centered workflows; the field shifted rapidly from in‑person to online proctoring with little guidance on choosing proctoring types for diverse learners</cite>.
- BYOD success depends on supervision capacity and venue availability, not just software. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Feasibility was limited mainly by venue capacity and supervision resources, without increasing grading workload</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Lockdown browsers and automated video proctoring are common controls, but they increase client device demands and introduce new failure surfaces</cite>.

2) Device heterogeneity and connectivity/power constraints
- BYOD exams can be “secure” only if institutions standardize the environment; otherwise, uneven OS/browser versions, local network bandwidth, battery life, and hardware capability drive uneven performance and reliability. <cite id="330c8581-3">Technical issues were mainly software‑related and the system was vulnerable to the low quality of personal gear</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Safe Exam Browser and related lockdown approaches restrict unauthorized software and internet access, but require disciplined client configuration and monitoring</cite>.
- Network and power are not optional for hundreds to thousands of devices. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Institutions should invest in secure and robust infrastructure, including reliable wireless connectivity and power solutions</cite>. Absent such controls, BYOD exams suffer from dropped sessions, slow load times, and abrupt shutdowns during invigilation.

3) Accessibility, accommodations, and integrity trade‑offs
- BYOD and remote proctoring can conflict with disability‑related accommodations and principles of equitable design; institutions without mature accessibility processes risk legal and pedagogical harm even as they deploy integrity tools. <cite id="c05e43de-0">A decade of experience in disability‑related testing accommodations led to a framework for equitable online proctoring and negotiated vendor practices</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-1">BYOD success requires meticulous setup: tailored exercise variants, anomaly detection, and accommodations (time extensions, special seating) via examination boards to ensure fairness</cite>. <cite id="c05e43de-2">Faculty worry about “unfair advantages” when remote arrangements alter timing, while eye control by proctors can be circumvented by concealed smartphones; online campus invigilation raises new self‑assistance risks</cite>.
- Lockdown and video proctoring can impede accessibility or create undue stress; without parallel in‑person or alternative modality accommodations, BYOD risks violating UDL and anti‑discrimination obligations. <cite id="c0a3d29a-2">Automated video proctoring detects screen changes to infer movement outside the window, adding usability burdens and potential misclassification risks for disabled students</cite>.

4) Integrity vs. learning outcomes and fairness trade‑offs
- Aggressive proctoring and monitoring can lower performance or inflate anxiety, undermining validity and equity. <cite id="c0a3d29a-4">Students performed 10–20% better but took roughly twice as long on non‑proctored vs. proctored exams; the effect persisted when comparing the same exam proctored vs. non‑proctored</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-3">Supervisor apps accurately detected suspicious events without affecting exam performance, but the system’s efficiency was low and technical issues could interrupt exams</cite>. Institutions that push continuous, intrusive monitoring without compensating for usability and time burdens risk depressing scores and alienating students.

5) Policy gaps, contingency planning, and vendor dependence
- BYOD policies that ignore device diversity, acceptable browsers/OS updates, emergency rollback, and student support lead to crisis management during invigilation. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Revising exam policies to include provisions and contingency plans for BYOD is crucial; supervisors should assist with technical issues and re‑routine students to labs if problems persist</cite>.

- Context and capacity shape guidance: “Pilot and iterate” vs. “deploy immediately with heavy monitoring”
  - Evidence from large cohorts shows that BYOD is feasible and can reduce dishonesty compared to fully remote proctored settings, but only with careful planning, supervision, and infrastructure—leading to a conservative, pilot‑first recommendation. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">BYOD showed reduced dishonesty compared to remote exams and is feasible at scale when venue capacity and supervision are adequate</cite>. <cite id="c0a3d29a-0">Pilots, training, robust infrastructure, supervision, and revised policies are recommended</cite>.

- Pedagogy and assessment design mediate technology choice
  - If exams are ill‑designed for device‑based work (e.g., copy‑pasteable resources), BYOD can increase invalid advantage; if well‑designed for higher‑order skills, BYOD can preserve validity. Title: Comparing Student Performance on Proctored and Non-Proctored Exams in Online Psychology Courses

Utilizing a sample of about 1,700 students who took online psychology classes of varying difficulty at Washington State University from the spring 2015 to spring 2016, we found that students performed 10-20% better but took about twice as long on non-proctored versus proctored exams. This confirmed our hypotheses and the effect held when we compared our in-house proctoring service used during this time against ProctorU used for one semester in the fall 2012. Title: Transforming Computer-Based Exams with BYOD: An Empirical Study
Snippet: Based on the experiences derived from the organization of multiple exams using the presented BYOD concept, coupled with the insights garnered from the survey, we strongly advocate the integration of BYOD exams as a valuable approach for programming education assessment. This endeavor is pivotal to ensure the seamless and effective execution of exams within the BYOD framework. 

The claim of increased cheating activities in BYOD exams cannot be substantiated. Throughout the three examinations, there was no discernible increase in cheating incidents. Effective examination systems mitigate such concerns by incorporating features such as tailored exercise variants for each student and facilitating instructors in promptly identifying irregularities in student submissions, including instances of plagiarism or discrepancies in session details like multiple IPs or browsers. Students facing concentration challenges can request special seating, while those with specific weaknesses or disabilities can seek individual time extensions and seating accommodations through the examination board. This is supported by the Artemis Exam Process. With appropriate examination room infrastructure and availability, combined with an effective exam system, BYOD exams can be seamlessly scaled to accommodate over 1500 students simultaneously. Artemis enhances the examination process for both students and instructors, offering familiar usability for students, while providing instructors with helpful features such as (semi-) automatic assessment, plagiarism detection, exercise variants, session anomaly detection, and more. 

Computer-based exams with BYOD emphasize applying knowledge at higher cognitive levels, moving beyond rote memorization or basic comprehension of course content. Consequently, instructors must exercise vigilance in crafting exams to strike an appropriate balance, ensuring they do not inadvertently become excessively challenging or lengthy due to the accessibility of support tools, the internet, and course resources. There is a latent risk of overestimating students' capacities in this context. As a safeguard, we recommend conducting a thorough review with a representative student, using tools such as Artemis' test run feature to refine the exam's design and structure. 

In case of technical issues, the supervisors should assist the students in resolving the problems. If the issue cannot be resolved, students should be sent to a computer lab to finish their exam there.

This article will help you identify the goals of your institution and provide a framework for analyzing proctoring tools.
